summary:
Article 567 of Burundi's Penal Code criminalises sexual relations between people of the same sex, and applies to conduct by both men and women. The provision was passed on 22 November 2008 and took effect on 22 April 2009; such conduct was not an offence before that date. Conviction carries three months to two years of imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 100,000 Burundian francs.

OutRight International's March 2026 country entry cites Article 250 of the Penal Code for the same offence, with up to two years in prison and a fine. The sources do not reconcile the two article numbers.

Burundi provides no legal gender recognition as of March 2026. A visitor cannot obtain local documents or identity markers matching their gender, and LGBTIQ organisations cannot register as associations.

Article 29 of the Constitution bans same-sex marriage. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised.

Documented enforcement starts on 1 July 2009, when a man in Bujumbura was arrested for being gay and police offered release in exchange for money; he was freed after advocacy intervened. Two women were briefly arrested in 2012 and released. In September 2014 a case in Karuzi Province involving a foreign company employee and a Burundian man was dropped after three days for lack of evidence.

On 2 November 2016 the High Court of Cibitoke Province sentenced a 15-year-old boy, who had admitted raping a seven-year-old boy, to one year in prison on charges of rape of a minor and homosexuality. The US State Department's reporting for 2016 states that no prosecutions for consensual same-sex conduct were reported that year, and that LGBT people faced societal discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity with no government protection from it.

Enforcement intensified in 2023. In March 2023, 24 people were arrested on same-sex conduct charges; that charge was dropped after one accused person died in detention, but seven defendants were convicted of inciting debauchery. In August 2023 seven people were sentenced to one to two years in prison for engaging in homosexual acts.

In December 2023 President Évariste Ndayishimiye said gay sex was like choosing Satan and that people found engaging in it should be taken to stadiums and stoned, and he rejected development aid conditioned on respecting LGBT rights. Human Rights Watch reported the remarks in January 2024. SOS Médias Burundi reported that LGBTQ Burundians described terror in their wake; the Iteka League, operating in exile, called the remarks a call for the lynching of LGBTQ people, and two members of LGBTQ associations speaking anonymously described them as a real license to kill us.

US State Department human rights reporting for 2009, 2010, 2012 and 2015 documents discrimination against gays and lesbians and, for 2015, arrests and harassment of LGBT persons. The 2015 report sets these findings within a documented national crisis that included extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detention and media shutdowns.

OutRight International's March 2026 entry reports harassment, discrimination, family rejection and stigmatisation of LGBTIQ people, in a setting it describes as including extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, arbitrary arrests, torture and sexual and gender-based violence, with no meaningful legal reform.

The most recent documented incident in this record is the January 2024 reporting on the president's December 2023 remarks; no later enforcement case or official statement is documented here.
tangentialFactors:
The 2015 US State Department report places its section on LGBT persons inside a broader account of crisis in Burundi covering extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detention and shutdowns of media. A visitor's exposure to state violence in this record is therefore not confined to the sexual-orientation offence itself.

The 2010 report lists discrimination against gays and lesbians among common human-rights abuses alongside security-force killings, torture and harsh prison conditions. The 2012 report pairs that discrimination finding with torture, extrajudicial executions and prolonged pretrial detention.

The November 2016 Cibitoke case shows a homosexuality charge layered onto a rape-of-minor charge against a child defendant, so the offence can be added to other counts rather than standing alone.

In December 2023 the president tied the issue to external relations by rejecting aid conditioned on respecting LGBT rights, which places official hostility in policy as well as rhetoric.

The Iteka League's operations from exile indicate that domestic space for organised advocacy on this issue is closed, leaving reporting dependent on outlets and organisations working outside the country.
localsOnly:
LGBTIQ organisations cannot register as associations in Burundi as of March 2026, so residents have no legally constituted body to join or to bring complaints collectively.

With no legal gender recognition available, residents cannot obtain identity documents or markers matching their gender, and there is no domestic procedure for changing them.

Article 29 of the Constitution bars same-sex marriage, and no partnership recognition of any kind follows from it.

Government protection from discrimination is absent: the US State Department's 2016 reporting states that LGBT people faced societal discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity without government protection from such discrimination.

OutRight International's March 2026 entry describes family rejection, stigmatisation and harassment as the resident experience, alongside arbitrary arrests and torture, and records no meaningful legal reform.

The March 2023 mass arrest produced acquittal on the same-sex conduct charge only after one accused person died in detention; seven co-defendants were nonetheless convicted of inciting debauchery. In August 2023 seven people received sentences of one to two years for homosexual acts.

The Iteka League, which characterised the president's December 2023 remarks as a call for lynching, works from exile rather than from inside Burundi.
outOfScopeNotes:
The article number for the offence is unresolved in the sources. Article 567, with its 2008 passage and 2009 commencement dates and its specific penalty range, is the provision given by the encyclopaedic and US State Department material; OutRight International's March 2026 entry instead cites Article 250 with a penalty of up to two years and a fine. Whether this reflects a recodification, a renumbering or an error is not sourced here.

The inventory contains no count of killings or violence against trans people in Burundi, and no general homicide rate to set beside one, so no trans-specific rate can be stated or compared with background violence.

No source in this inventory addresses entry or border practice: there is nothing on visa screening, secondary screening, pat-downs or inspection triggered by binders, packers, breast forms or gender presentation, nor on how a foreign passport's gender marker is treated at Burundian entry.

Nothing here covers access to gender-affirming healthcare, its legality, or any medical screening requirement for visitors.

The record documents no enforcement incident after the August 2023 sentences and no official statement after the December 2023 remarks reported in January 2024; the absence of later cases is a gap in sourcing, not a finding about present conditions.
